records.text: Fork. One piece is now hitting several targets at once, and the other side has some sorting out to do.
The other side gets a fork out of this. One of their pieces can reach several targets in a single move.
Another move had a fork going, one piece against several targets. This move leaves that on the table.
Pinned to the king. That piece now holds its line whether it likes it or not; moving off would expose the king behind it.
Now the other side has a pin against the king to work with. A pinned piece holds its line or the king is exposed.
A pin to the king was on offer in another move, freezing a piece on its line. This move passes it up.
Skewered. The front piece is under attack, and once it moves aside, whatever stood behind it on that line is exposed.
A skewer is now on offer to the other side. If the front piece moves off the line, whatever stands behind it may be exposed.
Another move had a skewer ready: move the front piece, and whatever stood behind it would have been exposed.
Capture the guard, and whatever it was guarding stands bare. That is the whole point of the move.
One of the defenders can now be captured. Whatever it guards may lose its protection along with it.
Another move would have removed a defender and stripped its charge of cover. Here that defender is left in place.
Its own pieces have the king boxed in. The back rank is where this move collects.
The king's own pieces are sitting on its escape squares. The other side now has a back-rank mate to aim for.
Another move had a back-rank mate, against a king stuck behind its own pieces. This move strolls on by.
This pawn is running for the last rank, where it turns into a new piece. Promotion is the threat.
A pawn of theirs is now in the running for promotion. Pawns that reach the last rank stop being pawns.
A stronger move cleared a pawn's way to promotion. This move keeps that road closed.
One piece clears the line, and the piece it was screening gets to attack. Discovered attack, textbook.
One of their pieces is standing in front of another. If it moves, the piece behind gets a clear line. A discovered attack, available to them.
Another move would have unmasked an attack by shifting the piece in front. This move leaves the mask on.
One move, carrying two demands. A double attack, and each demand needs an answer.
The other side can make two threats with a single move now. A double attack, and both will need answering.
A stronger move would have hit two targets in a single turn. This move leaves that double attack unplayed.
Deflection: a defender gets hauled away, and whatever it was covering now stands unguarded.
One defender is doing a vital job. The other side can now drag it away from that job: a deflection, theirs to use.
Another move would have pried a defender loose from its job. That chance at deflection goes begging.
That piece has no guard at all. Take it. Nothing more complicated than that.
An undefended piece was available to another move. This one leaves it standing. Loose pieces get billed.
This leaves a piece hanging, free for the other side to take. They will not need an invitation.
A piece is there for the taking now. This move walked its only real defender off the job. Costly, that.
A piece is now open to capture. The opponent's last move made a threat, and this move lets it stand.
The capture looks fine until the recapture, which takes a more valuable piece. An exchange is judged at the end, not the start.
A minor piece is developed, off its starting square and working.
The alternative developed a minor piece instead.
Open file, rook on it. Not a pawn of either color on the whole file.
White's rook is on an open file now. No pawns. That is the definition, not a promise.
Black's rook is on an open file now. No pawns. That is the definition, not a promise.
The alternative was a rook on an open file, a file without a single pawn.
The better move would have put White's rook on a file without pawns. Open, not necessarily vacant.
The better move would have put Black's rook on a file without pawns. Open, not necessarily vacant.
The rook now works a semi-open file: none of its own pawns there, at least one of the enemy's.
Half-open file for White's rook. Enemy pawns remain there; friendly pawns do not.
Half-open file for Black's rook. Enemy pawns remain there; friendly pawns do not.
A semi-open file was available to a rook with another move: its own pawns gone from the file, an enemy pawn still there.
White's rook would have had a half-open file with the better move. Enemy pawns only; not an empty file.
Black's rook would have had a half-open file with the better move. Enemy pawns only; not an empty file.
That pawn is passed; no enemy pawn stands in front of it on its file or either neighbor. Worth watching.
White now has a passed pawn. Passed, not unstoppable.
Black now has a passed pawn. Passed, not unstoppable.
A passed pawn was available to another move, free of enemy pawns ahead on its file and both neighbors.
The better move would have given White a passer. Worth including in the calculation.
The better move would have given Black a passer. Worth including in the calculation.
One step closer to the last rank for the passed pawn.
The passed pawn moves nearer promotion. Nearer is not there.
A passer advances. Less distance remains; that does not remove the opposition.
The alternative pushed the passed pawn forward, nearer the last rank.
That pawn is isolated now. No friendly pawn on either neighboring file to keep it company.
White has an isolated pawn now. No friendly pawns on the adjacent files. Pieces may still help.
Black has an isolated pawn now. No friendly pawns on the adjacent files. Pieces may still help.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, without a friendly pawn on either file beside it.
The stronger alternative would have isolated a pawn for White. Better moves can have untidy details.
The stronger alternative would have isolated a pawn for Black. Better moves can have untidy details.
That piece was on its own. Not anymore; it has a guard.
Covering the loose piece was the alternative. Cheap insurance.
This piece has no defender now. Undefended is a condition, not a verdict.
With another move, a piece would have stood undefended. By itself, that would not have cost it.
An escape square opens up for the king, legal and available. Escape routes are cheaper to build before they are needed.
The alternative gave the king a fresh legal flight square.
Castling done: the king steps aside and the rook comes into play; two pieces moved, one tempo spent.
King two squares over, rook shifted. Castling, in one move.
The alternative was castling, which shifts king and rook with a single move.
With this capture, one side's bishop pair is history. It keeps bishops on only one color now.
The alternative took a bishop and split up the other side's pair.
Two pawns of one color on one file: doubled.
Doubled pawns for White. Same file; no automatic disaster attached.
Doubled pawns for Black. Same file; no automatic disaster attached.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, two of one color stacked on a single file.
White's pawns would have shared a file after the better move. Doubled does not settle the argument.
Black's pawns would have shared a file after the better move. Doubled does not settle the argument.
Forced checkmate is now available to the other side. The defense around the king has run out. Follow the mating line from here.
There was a forced mate in the position. This move passes it up. Unfinished business.
Courtesy of this move, the other side may checkmate on their very next turn. Prompt service.
Forced checkmate from here. The defense can try anything. Ordered, not yet delivered.
Still forcing mate. This move keeps the arrangement in place. The booking stands.
Mate's still forced. Some other move would have been quicker about it. Scenic route, same destination.
The reply doesn't matter; this side's next turn is mate. Nothing left to negotiate.
Mate was unavoidable for the side that just moved. This move hurries it along. Stiffer resistance would have stalled it.
Mate can't be stopped. No searched alternative postpones it beyond this move. When the result is fixed, delay is the only defense left.
The material is on offer, and taking it does not refute the sacrifice, not in the line searched. The offer has teeth.
Every other searched move was losing. This one kept the game playable. No room for anything else.
Everything else checked lost. This held. Efficient.
This kept the position playable. Nothing else checked managed that. Tidy work.
Only one survivor among the moves checked. This one. The others lost.
This move holds on to the advantage. Nothing else searched did; the rest were losing.
The reply has a capture available immediately. Check what it costs.
An immediate capture is available to the other side. Profit still requires calculation.
The opponent can capture on the next move. Available does not mean free.
A capture can come straight back. Include it in the arithmetic.
The reply may take something immediately. Check the result before celebrating it.
The reply can take the pawn immediately. Count the cost.
The other side can capture the knight next move. Check the bill.
The bishop can be taken straight away. Do the arithmetic on that.
An immediate capture of the rook is available to the opponent. Price it.
The opponent can take the queen at once. Worth knowing what that costs.
The best answer for the other side gives check. Everything else waits until the king is dealt with.
The strongest reply checks the king. That takes precedence.
Best reply: check. Resolve the king's problem first.
The engine prefers a different move. Put the two side by side and compare the replies; that is where they differ.
Another move was stronger. It deserves the comparison.
There is a better alternative to put beside this choice.
The move not played offered more. Compare that option.
This costs something against the engine's best move. The reply presents the bill.
A worse position than the better move offered. That difference is the cost.
The stronger choice gives a better position. This move falls short.
Less than was available. Put the stronger move beside this one; the comparison matters.
The position pays for this choice relative to the best move. The difference warrants attention.
Strong, and economical about it. Next to anything the engine searched, almost nothing is conceded.
Sound. The engine has a preference, but most of the value is still there.
Theory knows this line. Known territory, for now.
Theory runs out here. No more book past this point; calculation from here on.
The earlier setback has been dealt with. With this move, the position is playable again.
The earlier setback no longer decides things; the position is playable again. Their mistakes lent a hand. Help is help.
The opponent's last move opened a gap. This move cashes it in. As it should.
You punished the last error. The opponent supplied it; you used it.
That makes use of the opponent's mistake. A chance properly collected.
The previous error costs the opponent now. You did not let it pass.
The opponent's last move put something on the table. This move leaves it there.
This issue already turned up earlier in the game. Same warning sign, again. Compare those moments.
The earlier unguarded piece has its guard back. Repaired.
No single disaster. Small concessions, one after another, and this is another one. They add up.
The advantage stayed in hand right up to the recorded win. Converted, without handing any of it back.
The same issue is on file in other saved games. It has a history. Study them together.
Mate, and final. Not one legal move left for that king.
It ends in checkmate, the king without a legal move. The lesson sits earlier, in the defense.
Drawn. Nobody collects. The earlier decisions are still worth a look.
Take in the position. Then move.
That fails. Check the reply before trusting the next attempt.
That attempt returned nothing. Enter the move a second time.
The saved engine analysis has a forced checkmate here, for the side that made this move.
After this move, the saved engine analysis has a forced checkmate. For the other side.

When the saved line is over, the side that made this move has lost material, measured against the start of that line.
This exercise accepts the move. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves given, so none is claimed.
No acceptance for this move in this exercise. No clear tactical reason shows in the moves given, and none is invented.
This matches a saved answer. For this exercise, the saved answers decide.

Practice saved, review schedule untouched.
Solved, though the relearning mark stays.
The starting position, before any of these moves are played.
Moving on. Look at what changed.
Check, and it gets answered before anything else.
With this move, the check is dealt with.
The pawn reaches the last rank and is promoted.
Promotion, with check attached.
The pawn promotes, and that is mate. Every move the king had is gone.
The pawn promotes, and the same move takes its own king out of check.
Something gets taken.
Takes a piece, gives check.
Takes a piece and mates. Every legal move the king had is gone.
Takes a piece, and the check is escaped by the same move.
The pawn takes on the last rank and becomes a new piece.
The pawn takes on the last rank, promotes, and checks the king, all with a single move.
Capturing onto the last rank, the pawn promotes, and that is mate.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, taking its own king out of check in the process.
The king castles, and the move gives check.
Castling delivers mate; the enemy king has no legal move.
The forking piece hits several targets and collects one. Here the fork ends with a net material gain.
That piece is not allowed to make the capture: it is pinned, and leaving the line would leave its own king in check, which is illegal.
The attacked piece cannot simply run, because its king sits behind it on the line. Whatever it does, the king has to stay covered.
No recapture is available: every defender is pinned against its king. In the line shown, material is won.
Stepping off its line would expose the king, so the pinned piece stays put. It does not survive these moves.
The front piece gets out of the way. Then the piece behind it gets taken, down the same line.
Check moves the king off the line by force. The same attacker then helps itself to the piece that stood behind.
Step one: the lone defender comes off. Later in these moves, whatever it guarded follows.
The defender is pulled off its job, and the piece it left is taken.
The blocker moves. Another piece captures down the line it opened.
One piece moves aside, unmasking a check from the piece it was hiding.
That is double check: two attackers on the king, and only a king move answers that.
The moving piece attacks once and unmasks a second attack. Here the second piece collects its target.
The pawn promotes, and that side finishes this example with a net material gain.
A piece nobody guarded comes off the board. The side that took it ends the example up material, net.
The attacking piece was held in a relative pin until the opponent's previous move released it. Nobody moved the target after that, and by the end of the line shown, it is gone.
The marked reply belongs to the other side. Put it on the board and watch what it does.

Before a quiet move, look for enemy pieces nobody is guarding.
Look at forcing moves where one piece hits two valuable targets.

Before trading off a defender, know exactly what it protects.
When a blocking piece moves, follow every line it uncovers.
Hunt for a move carrying two demands. Checks and newly opened lines count.
Before a back-rank defender moves, know where the king can escape.
Count the moves between the pawn and promotion. Then check every forcing push.
A defender that moves takes its protection with it. Know what that covers first.
First, the value the capture wins. Then, the value the recapture takes back. The difference is the price.
Check whether a forcing exchange can drag a defender off something else it guards.

This line assumes strong replies. Not all of them are forced.
